newsitem.title: FRANCE: French oil refining investments to fall - ministry.
newsitem.headline: French oil refining investments to fall - ministry.

text.p: Investment in French oil refineries is set to fall by 15 percent in 1997 -- and then tumble by another 40 percent by 1999 -- as the oil business weighs up an uncertain future in refining, an official French poll shows.

Research compiled by the French industry ministry suggests the amount of money ploughed into refineries in 1999 will be barely a third of its three billion franc peak in 1994 -- but plans could be revised if the current poor climate improves.

"Provisional budgets for coming years have in general been under-estimated, particularly for 1999, because of uncertainties over the future of French and European refining caused by economic and environmental constraints," the ministry's oil directorate said in an industry note received on Monday.
The constraints include a glut of refining capacity in Europe, weak refining margins and increasingly strict controls on the emissions from refined products like diesel fuel.

The industry ministry, which is responsible for France's nuclear-dominated energy sector, carried out its research by looking at the spending plans for 17 private oil or chemical plants, including the country's 13 fully operating refineries.
It said that on current plans, total downstream oil investment would fall to 1.853 billion francs in 1997 from 2.170 billion francs in 1997.
It would carry on falling to 1.426 billion francs in 1998 and then 1.118 billion francs in 1999.
The ministry said it could not give budgets for individual plants because of the secrecy involved in oil company planning.
But it cautioned one of the reasons for falling investment was the large sum of money the industry had already spent on boosting the octane content in petrol between 1990 and 1994.
In 1992, measures to produce extra high-performance octane gobbled up around one billion francs or more than a third of the total downstream investments in France, the ministry said.
By 1999, that figure should have fallen to 10 million francs or less than one percent of the total.

Spending on desulphurisation units has also been falling, although not at the same dramatic pace as for octane. This year will be crucial for deciding whether new-style plants will be efficient enough to carry the industry beyond the year 2000, when the European Union may call for a further tightening of emission standards, the French ministry said.
Spending on conversion facilities used to make high-value oil products has held up relatively well and may be under-estimated in budgets for the years ahead, it added.
The report is being circulated to oil firms just as several of them face the biggest potential shake-up in French refining for several years, in a drive to soak up excess capacity.

Oil companies operating a cluster of refineries around Marseilles in southern France -- an area seen facing one of the worst problems of overcapacity in Europe -- have said they are working on an idea for joint rationalisation to be presented to the industry ministry by the end of the month.
Royal Dutch/Shell, which operates the Berre refinery near Marseilles, said two weeks ago it was talking to other operators and was confident of reaching an agreement.
Esso France, Total SA and BP France also run plants in the area. BP has put its Lavera refinery up for sale despite the talks.
